newsitem.title: USA: AIG denies pulled out of muni swap business.
newsitem.headline: AIG denies pulled out of muni swap business.

text.p: American International Group Thursday said it has scaled back its unit offering interest rate swaps and other derivatives to U.S. municipalities, denying a spate of media reports that it closed the operation.

The company's derivatives subsidiary, AIG Financial Products, "continues to execute unique and creative business opportunities with municipal clients," spokesman John Wooster said. The company declined to comment on the status of the unit when the stories were written in September.
The financial products company has scaled back its municipal unit laying off some staff, Wooster acknowledged.

Officials at other firms in the market continued to say, however, that AIG has significantly reduced its presence in munis. Other firms have also pulled back, in part because of reduced issuance of municipal bonds since 1993.
Wooster also defended the performance of the financial products subsidiary, which has done business with a broad range of clients in the past, including municipalities, corporations and banks.
The company revealed in a routine filing Wednesday that the value of its swaps with municipalities declined by $300 million this year.

"In the third quarter AIGFP's net operating income was up 62 percent," Wooster responded. "They're having an excellent year. Wooster declined to discuss the performance of specific business segments such as municipal swaps.
In the filing, AIG said the net replacement value of its swaps with municipalities dropped to $579 million from $880 million, or 34 percent, from December 31, 1995, to September 30, 1996.
Replacement value indicates the current value of the swaps -- the estimated cost to AIG if its swap counterparties defaulted and it had to replace the positions in the current market.

"That this measure of credit exposure declined significantly simply reflects the one percent rise in U.S. interest rates during the period," the company said in a statement. The decline is a measure of credit exposure not an "economic loss," the company said.

The losses may never be realized. The positions remain open and the market could rise in the future. Also, the company tries to use offsetting transactions to hedge its exposure, which provide offsetting gains when the swaps decline in value.

"There is absolutely no income effect of these changes on AIGFP whatsoever," the company said. The subsidiary reported operating income of $130 million on net trading revenues of $287 million for the first nine months of the year.
The replacement value of all of the unit's derivatives with non-municipal counterparties dropped to $5.3 billion from $6.0 billion, or 12 percent, over the same period.

AIG has not been contacted or subpoenaed in relation to a U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission investigation of its largest swap with a municipality, a $422 million swap with Dade County, Florida, Wooster added.
